https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c65y.text: Figure caption, Watch: Israeli settlers attack Palestinians in West Bank during olive harvest By Lucy Williamson Middle East correspondent ,Â Reporting from Abu Falah Published 5 hours ago Dozens of masked settlers have attacked Palestinians and set fire to cars and olive trees during the annual olive harvest in the occupied West Bank. A BBC team witnessed one of several attacks in farmland near the Palestinian village of Abu Falah. A local official said the attacks had injured 12 Palestinians, including four dual Palestinian American citizens. A foreign journalist was also among those hurt. Driving into the area early in the morning, we came across the first signs of the violence : a stream of cars carrying wounded Palestinian olive farmers racing out along the narrow stony track, piled high with olive picking equipment, as smoke rose from several fires nearby. The bloodied face of Majdi Fheed peered out from the backseat of one car. "We were getting our olive trees and almost 15 Jewish guys â¦ started attacking us with guns, with rocks, with special weapons. They hit me on my head [and] my neck â look, I am bleeding!" Yaser AlKam, a council member from the neighbouring village of Turmus Aya told me Majdi - an American citizen - was attacked by settlers with nail-studded sticks, and needed treatment for deep wounds on his head. His elderly mother was also injured. Another man ferrying the injured to hospital told us that settlers had attacked them with sticks while they harvested their olives, and had burned three cars â including one of his own. "As soon as we got to the land and put our things on the ground, they started to come, so we ran away" said a woman next to him. Image caption, Several Palestinian-American citizens and a foreign journalist were left injured following the attack Asked about the violence, a US State Department spokesperson said they were aware of the reports. "Weâ¯condemn criminalâ¯violenceâ¯by any partyâ¯in the West Bank and call for investigations, arrests, and convictions,â¯of those responsible," the spokesperson said. Watching the vehicles stream past her, 73-year-old Imm Khaldoun told me emphatically that, no matter what happened, she would always return to her land. "This is my land. It's my right [to be here]" she told me. The UN says the past two weeks have already seen more attacks by violent Israeli settlers than during the entire harvest season last year. Olive picking in the West Bank is now a test of speed, with trees rapidly stripped of fruit as soon as the sun rises, before violent Israeli settlers attack. In another olive orchard nearby, we watched as dozens of farmers used power-tools to strip the trees as fast as they could â one eye on the ridge above us, where a group of settlers at a new illegal outpost had already gathered, and were watching the olive harvest below. Standing on ladders, the Palestinian farmers worked quickly, sending streams of olives onto the plastic sheets laid out under the trees. Three villages had come together to harvest these olives, the landowner Amin Khalil, told me, as a form of protection against attack. He said his land was now surrounded by seven Jewish settlements and outposts. Image caption, Yaser AlKam was left bloodied from the attack All Israeli settlements are illegal under international law. Outposts â small encampments on hilltops â are illegal under Israeli law as well, but many still receive state support. "This is a hotspot â there are seven settlements around here," Amin Khalil told me. "This year, all the people came together because when there are just a few people working alone at the edge of the village, the settlers attack. So all the families are working together today." But the tactic doesn't work today. As we watch, dozens of settlers, all dressed in black, begin moving down the hill towards us, setting fire to several groups of olive trees. There are shouts of panic from the Palestinian farmers, yelling for children to get out of the field. Some begin swiftly wrapping up the olives to leave. But with large numbers of people on both sides, the confrontation stalls into an uneasy stalemate. We see settlers with slingshots hurl stones towards us, and young Palestinian men running to throw stones in return. As Israeli forces arrive, the standoff explodes into action. Settlers begin running down towards us as the farmers swiftly retreat. Some Palestinians set off fireworks to try and push the settlers back. Image source, Reuters Image caption, The UN says settler attacks this year have so far killed one Palestinian and injured more than 120 others American journalist Heidi Levine of the Washington Post was injured in the attack. She described how dozens of settlers ambushed her as she was reporting at the scene. "I got jumped," she said. "I was on the ground and they were kicking me and I was trying to hold onto my camera and my bag. I had my helmet and flak jacket on which protected me. They made me stand up and they kicked me again, and this went on for at least 10 minutes." In a statement, Washington Post executive editor Matt Murray said Levine had been clearly identifiable as a journalist. "We are outraged by this unwarranted attack on a journalist doing her job and urge a thorough investigation and follow-through from authorities," he said. The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) said personnel had been despatched to the area "following a report of a violent confrontation". It said a female journalist had been injured during the confrontation. And that "all circumstances" surrounding the incident would be examined. As the farmers retreated, the sound of live ammunition cracked across the fields. It was unclear if settlers or Israeli forces were firing. Minutes later, Israeli forces began firing tear gas into the Palestinian fields to end the confrontation â a well-worn Israeli pattern of managing these conflicts. The UN says settler attacks on the olive harvest this year have so far killed one Palestinian and injured more than 120 others across the West Bank. Illegal Jewish outposts have mushroomed here over the past few years, clustering in closer around Palestinian olive groves. What we witnessed was part of a pattern being repeated day after day, as settler outposts here increase. The yearly olive harvest has become a litmus test of how the policies of Israel's fiercely pro-settlement government are affecting Palestinians here, by presiding over growing violence by extremist settlers, and fuelling Jewish claims to the land. The protesters called for the scrapping of the SIR exercise, alleging it could disenfranchise voters. According to a participant, hundreds of people had gathered for the march from Connaught Place to the Election Commission of India (ECI) headquarters. Indian authorities crack down on 'Cockroach' protest To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video According to the Hindustan Times newspaper, the police detained some of the protesters who were marching to the ECI office. India's youth-led Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), along with other organizations and opposition parties have demanded the resignation of Kumar after a newspaper investigation alleged impropriety during a large-scale voter-roll revision. According to the probe, published in The Indian Express newspaper, some key decisions linked to the SIR of voter rolls that began last year were likely taken without the approval of two of the three election commissioners. The CJP has laid out three demands : Kumar's resignation and criminal proceedings against him, a freeze on the SIR and the suspension of all upcoming elections, and the repeal of the 2023 law on the appointment of the election commissioners of India. The Election Commission has rejected allegations of internal disagreements over the SIR process, saying major decisions were taken unanimously by the full commission. India-Israel relations have flourished under Modi: In 2017, Modi became the first ever prime minister of India to visit Israel In February 2026, became the first Indian Prime Minister to address the Knesset https://p.dw.com/p/5OZjO Skip next section Hindu nationalist group to protest Elon Musk's Starlink in Delhi 10/23/2026 October 23, 2026 Hindu nationalist group to protest Elon Musk's Starlink in Delhi An organization affiliated with India's Hindu nationalist Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS) movement will hold a protest march in New Delhi on Friday against SpaceX founder Elon Musk's Starlink, citing national security and digital sovereignty concerns. The Swadeshi Jagran Manch (SJM) said the march would begin at 11 a.m. (0530 GMT) in the capital's Chanakyapuri area. It has urged the government to block Starlink's commercial satellite broadband launch, arguing that its network could complicate internet shutdowns and lawful interception during security emergencies. The campaign follows Musk’s criticism of regulatory delays facing Starlink in India and his accusation that Reliance Industries, led by Indian billionaire Mukesh Ambani, is using its market power to block foreign competitors. In a tweet addressing Ambani as the Prime Minister of India and the "real boss of India," Musk accused the tycoon of "monopolistic exploitation" of Indians and keeping Starlink out of the market. Reliance has rejected the allegations. "It is unfortunate that instead of responding to the information requested from his company on national security grounds, Elon Musk chose to indirectly accuse Indian businesses and the government," the SJM said in a statement on its website. The SJM highlighted Starlink in Ukraine as a case study for national security. According to a Wall Street Journal report, the trillionaire ordered the slowdown of a military-grade version of SpaceX's Starlink satellite service that Kyiv relies on. Separately, in a sign of Musk's plummeting popularity in India, recently, controversial Dussehra posters displayed in the northern Lucknow city depicted Musk and other international figures, including US Senator Ilhan Omar, as the ten faces of Ravana, portraying them as opponents of India's interests. During the Hindu Dussehra festival effigies of Ravana are traditionally burned symbolizing the victory of good over evil. The Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) said the Indian Embassy in Riyadh and Consulate in Jeddah were coordinating with airlines and tour operators to arrange their return. Around 3,000 stranded Umrah pilgrims had returned to India on available flights over the past week, alongside more than 10,000 other Umrah pilgrims who travelled on scheduled services, according to the ministry statement. Umrah refers to the pilgrimage to Islam's holiest sites outside of the month of Dhul-Hijja. "Arrangements are being discussed to facilitate the return of other Umrah pilgrims at the earliest," the ministry said. Earlier, All India Majlis-e-Ittehadul Muslimeen (AIMIM) leader Asaduddin Owaisi had said around 4,000 Indian pilgrims were stranded in Mecca and Medina after Indian carriers cancelled flights. As Saudi Arabia's revived war with the Iranian-backed Houthi rebels has intensified in recent weeks, with the Yemeni rebels targeting several major Saudi airports , some Indians have found themselves caught in the middle. On Wednesday, one Indian national was killed and two others injured in an attack on Dammam airport in Saudi Arabia, while another was injured in an attack on the Shaybah oil field. Can Yemen's government turn the tide against the Houthis?
